entities.summary:
Carlo Barabino (died 1835) was the preeminent Neoclassical architect of Genoa, transforming its urban fabric and public spaces in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. His work, deeply rooted in the rationalist principles of the Enlightenment and inspired by ancient Roman forms, defined the city's monumental character during a period of profound political upheaval, spanning the final years of the Genoese Republic, the Napoleonic era, and the Restoration under the Kingdom of Sardinia. Barabino's vision laid the groundwork for modern urban planning in Genoa, leaving an indelible mark on its civic and cultural infrastructure.

Barabino's architectural output was prolific and diverse. Among his most significant commissions was the design of the Teatro Carlo Felice, inaugurated in 1828, a grand opera house that quickly became a cultural landmark and a symbol of Genoese civic pride, though much of it was later destroyed in World War II. He also conceived the initial plan for the monumental cemetery of Staglieno, a project he began in 1835 but did not live to complete, which would later become one of Europe's most renowned examples of monumental funerary architecture. His urban interventions included the redesign of Piazza Corvetto and the construction of the Accademia Ligustica di Belle Arti, completed in 1831, fostering artistic education and cultural development in the region.
